problem: Prior multi-agent RL work on hide-and-seek uses game-engine state rather than pixels and does not explain why useful representations emerge. It is unclear how learning from egocentric, partially observed vision produces representations of other agents.
motivation: Learning a policy from pixels alone provides only indirect reward supervision, yet it might force the network to learn scene-dynamics representations such as predator perspective and own visibility. The paper asks what structure in the game causes such features to emerge, by comparing hider variants with different advantages and weaknesses.
key_idea: Train a prey agent from scratch with PPO on egocentric pixels in a Unity hide-and-seek game, then probe its features and show that moderate agent weaknesses (e.g. slower speed) produce the richest emergent representations.
insight: Survival performance and representation quality are not monotonically related: the fitted parabola shows the best self-visibility features come from intermediate disadvantages. The strongest agent (visibilityreward+faster) has the worst probe accuracy (63.17% self-visibility vs 60.00% random-init), while stochasticseeker, stochasticmaps and visibilityreward reach about 95%. Too severe a weakness (slowerhider, 1.03% success) derails learning, and too strong an agent only learns a reactive policy.
method: Environment: Unity 3D 14x14 arena with obstacles; hider and seeker each see a 120° egocentric view, use 5 discrete actions (forward, backward, left, right, stand), run at 50 fps, and start facing each other.
Seeker policy: hand-coded deterministic (chase if visible, go to last known position, else round-robin waypoints), with a stochastic random-waypoint variant.
Hider policy: 3-conv + FC actor-critic CNN trained from scratch with PPO (Adam, lr 3e-4, 8e6 steps, 6-step action repeat); reward +0.001 per living step and -1 on capture.
Interventions: hider speed (slowerhider, fasterhider with acceleration), an auxiliary visibility reward of ±0.001, a stochastic seeker, and stochastic maps with random obstacles.

Representation probing: linear/logistic regression on mid-level features to predict seeker visibility (seeker recognition) and hider visibility (self-visibility), using ground-truth labels only after training, compared against a random-init policy.
Behavior analysis: visual-state visitation frequencies (S, H, O), state-transition probabilities, and inter-agent distance over time, computed from privileged game state for analysis only.

setting.backbone: 4-layer CNN + FC actor-critic (trained from scratch with PPO)
setting.training_data: Self-generated RL experience in the Unity hide-and-seek environment, 8M steps per variant; no external data
setting.action_space: 5 discrete actions (forward, backward, turn left, turn right, stand still), 6-step action repeat
setting.privileged: none for the policy; ground-truth game state used only for probing labels and analysis

numbers.eval_set_note: 100 rollout episodes per variant, max 1,000 steps

numbers.extra: auxiliary visibility reward; probe accuracy: seeker recognition 95.75%, self-visibility 94.92%

numbers_note: Custom Unity task, not a standard navigation benchmark. Probe accuracies for the other variants are in Table 3; the state-frequency and transition results are given only in figures.
results: All hiders beat the random policy, and the stronger agents survive longer (basic 500 steps / 45.36% success, fasterhider 526 steps, slowerhider 73 steps / 1.03%). Probing shows features encode seeker presence and self-visibility above random-init features. The best probe accuracies come from stochasticseeker, stochasticmaps and visibilityreward (about 95% self-visibility), not from the best survivors.
limitations: Failures come from the lack of memory (of the map and of past predator locations), since the policy is a feedforward CNN.

Simple, single-seeker Unity environment with a hand-coded seeker, and the game has an exploitable design flaw; conclusions rest on a small set of variants and 100 evaluation episodes, and the parabola fit is qualitative.
The paper only shows an association between weakness and representation quality, not a causal mechanism.
compares_to: Emergent tool use from multi-agent autocurricula (Baker et al., concurrent)
